m: Error bars that account for users being measured many times, instead of pretending every row is a fresh person.

m: Run the experiment with both arms identical. Any 'winner' you see is your false-positive rate showing up.

m: The chance your test detects a real effect of a given size. Usually targeted at 80%.
w: Before launch, paired with MDE. An underpowered test that shows nothing has told you nothing.

w: Paired with power. 'We saw no difference' is only meaningful next to the MDE you could have seen.

m: Budgeting your false-positive allowance across several planned peeks at the data.
w: How to look early without the peeking problem — you decide the schedule up front.

m: Writing the hypothesis, metric and stopping rule down before seeing any data.

m: A confidence interval for a proportion that behaves sanely at tiny counts and near 0% or 100%.

m: Extreme measurements drift back toward average on their own, with no intervention needed.

m: How common the thing is before you see any evidence.

m: Two things stop being related once you know a third.
w: The assumption underneath Naive Bayes, and the thing a DAG question is really testing.

m: Predictors so correlated that the model cannot tell their effects apart.

m: People click the top result because it is on top, not because it is better.

w: A far more sensitive ranking comparison than a standard A/B, using a fraction of the traffic.

m: All the vectors you can actually reach by combining a matrix's columns.
w: Why Ax=b sometimes has no solution — b simply is not in there. Least squares is the fallback.

m: Describing the same vector with a different set of axes.
w: Eigendecomposition and PCA are both this: pick axes where the problem is easy.

m: A set of axes where the matrix only stretches, never rotates.
w: Why diagonalisation makes repeated multiplication cheap — powers become powers of scalars.

m: Every symmetric matrix has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors and real eigenvalues.
w: The guarantee that makes PCA work at all — covariance matrices are symmetric.

m: The amount a matrix stretches a given direction; maximised by the top eigenvector.
w: Where the 'PCA finds the direction of maximum variance' claim comes from.

m: Rank plus null-space dimension equals the number of columns. Nothing is lost, only moved.
w: The one-line explanation of why a rank-deficient matrix has infinitely many solutions.

m: Axes that are mutually perpendicular and all of length one.
w: Why Q in QR is nice: its inverse is its transpose, so solving is cheap and numerically stable.

m: A vector scaled to length one — direction with the magnitude thrown away.
w: Cosine similarity is just a dot product of two of these.

m: Scaling some vectors and adding them up. The only operation in the subject.
w: Span, basis and rank are all defined in terms of it.

m: Splitting a matrix into perpendicular directions and an upper-triangular rest.
w: The numerically stable way to solve least squares — the one libraries actually use.

m: A fast triangular factorisation that only works on symmetric positive-definite matrices.
w: Twice as fast as LU when it applies — covariance matrices, Gaussian sampling, ridge regression.

m: Swapping rows during elimination so you never divide by something tiny.
w: The reason textbook Gaussian elimination is numerically unstable and the library version is not.

m: The AᵀA x = Aᵀb form of least squares.
w: Mathematically correct, numerically poor — it squares the condition number. Say QR instead.

m: The closest thing to an inverse for a matrix that has none.
w: How least squares is written in one line, and what lstsq returns.

m: Keeping only the largest singular values and discarding the rest.
w: Compression, denoising, and latent-semantic-style embeddings.

m: Rebuilding a matrix from a few directions instead of all of them.
w: The idea under LoRA, under PCA, and under most compression arguments.

m: The theorem proving truncated SVD is the best possible low-rank approximation.
w: The formal backing when you claim SVD is optimal, not just convenient.

m: How much a matrix stretches each of its principal directions.
w: Their ratio is the condition number; their squares are PCA's explained variance.

m: The share of total variance a component accounts for.
w: How you pick k in PCA, and the scree-plot elbow argument.

m: A table of how each pair of features moves together.
w: PCA eigendecomposes it. Whitening inverts it.

m: Transforming features so they have unit variance and no correlation.
w: Preprocessing before some distance-based methods; also what batch norm approximates cheaply.

m: Splitting one big matrix into two thin ones whose product approximates it.
w: Classical collaborative filtering, and the shape LoRA borrows.

m: A compact notation for specifying exactly which indices to multiply and sum.
w: Attention written in one line; the thing interviewers ask you to read, not write.

m: Flat spots that curve up in one direction and down in another.
w: The real obstacle in high-dimensional optimisation — not local minima, which are rare.

m: Computing all gradients in one backward sweep, cheap when outputs are few and inputs many.
w: Backpropagation is exactly this. Why training a billion parameters costs about two forward passes.

m: Least squares with a penalty on large coefficients. Shrinks everything, drops nothing.
w: The fix for multicollinearity, and the closed form that makes it Cholesky-friendly.

m: Least squares with an L1 penalty, which drives some coefficients exactly to zero.
w: When you want feature selection as part of fitting, not as a separate step.

m: Ridge and lasso mixed, so correlated features get selected as a group.
w: Lasso picks one of a correlated pair arbitrarily; elastic net keeps both.

m: Capping the gradient's size before the optimiser step.
w: Exploding gradients in RNNs and transformers. A loss that suddenly goes NaN is the symptom.

m: Halting training when validation loss stops improving.
w: Free regularisation. The follow-up: which checkpoint do you keep, and which split chose it?

m: Error plotted against training-set size, for train and validation.
w: How you tell underfitting from overfitting, and whether more data would help at all.

m: Cross-validation that keeps all rows from one entity in the same fold.
w: Any data with repeat users or patients — plain KFold leaks and flatters the score.

m: An inner loop for tuning, an outer loop for the honest score.
w: Why tuning and evaluating on the same folds gives an optimistic number.

m: Replacing a category with the mean outcome for that category.
w: High-cardinality categoricals. Leaks badly unless fitted inside the fold.

m: Dividing logits by one learned constant to fix overconfidence.
w: The simplest calibration method — one parameter, fitted on validation, accuracy unchanged.

m: Fitting a logistic regression on top of model scores to turn them into probabilities.
w: Calibrating an SVM or any model whose scores are not probabilities.
cards: Support Vector Machines & the Kernel Trick

m: Predicted probability on one axis, observed frequency on the other.
w: How you show a model is overconfident, rather than just asserting it.

m: The average gap between predicted confidence and actual accuracy across bins.
w: The single number for calibration. Bin count changes the answer, which is its weakness.

m: Mean squared error on probabilities — rewards being both correct and calibrated.
w: When accuracy hides a model that is right but wildly overconfident.

m: Matthews correlation coefficient — a balanced score that stays honest on skewed classes.
w: 99% negatives. Accuracy says 99%, MCC says near zero.

m: The loss that penalises confident wrong answers far more than hesitant ones.
w: The default classification loss, and what perplexity exponentiates.

m: How many options the model was effectively choosing between at each token.
w: Language-model quality in one number. Lower is better; it is exp(cross-entropy).

m: Two unrelated things: Linear Discriminant Analysis, or Latent Dirichlet Allocation.
w: Clarify which before answering — supervised dimensionality reduction, or topic modelling.

m: The model's own output changes the data it is next trained on.
w: Recommenders that narrow over time; fraud models that stop seeing what they block.

m: The ground truth arrives days or weeks after the prediction.
w: Churn, fraud, credit. It breaks naive monitoring and makes backtesting the only option.

m: The whole apparatus — dataset, metric, baseline, acceptance threshold — not a single score.
w: When you are asked how you would know the model got better.

m: A small, carefully labelled set treated as ground truth and changed rarely.
w: The regression suite for a model. The follow-up: who labelled it, and how do you stop it going stale?

m: Using a strong model to score another model's output.
w: Evaluating open-ended generation. The follow-up is always agreement with humans.

m: Checking the judge model against human labels before trusting its scores.
w: The answer to 'how do you know the judge is any good' — without it, the eval is decoration.

m: Whether the answer is actually supported by the retrieved passages.
w: RAG evaluation. Separate from whether the answer is correct — it can be both wrong and faithful.

m: Secondary metrics that must not get worse, even if the primary one improves.
w: Latency and complaint rate next to a conversion win. They stop you shipping a Pyrrhic victory.

m: Capability lost when a model is tuned to be safe and helpful.
w: The trade-off question on RLHF — refusals go up, raw benchmark scores sometimes go down.

m: Pre-agreed steps for giving up quality to stay available.
w: Designing for failure: full model, then smaller model, then cache, then static answer.

m: Keyword scoring that rewards rare words and discounts long documents.
w: The baseline a vector search must beat. Often it does not, on exact terms and product codes.

m: Running keyword and vector search together and merging the results.
w: The standard answer to 'semantic search missed an exact product name'.

m: A navigable graph index that finds near neighbours fast by skipping across layers.

m: Encoding query and item separately so item vectors can be precomputed.
w: How retrieval stays fast at scale — the cost of ranking millions is moved offline.

m: Prepending document context to each chunk before embedding it.
w: The fix for chunks that are meaningless alone — 'it rose 3%' with no subject.

m: No history yet for a new user or item, so personalisation has nothing to work with.
w: Every recommender design. The answer is content features or popularity until signal arrives.

m: Stripping personal data before text reaches a model or a log.
w: Any pipeline sending user content to a third-party API.

m: Applying permissions before search, not after.
w: Filtering after retrieval returns a short or empty list and leaks existence; pre-filtering is the correct design.

m: Reusing the computed attention state for a prompt prefix you have already seen.
w: Long system prompts repeated every call — cuts both latency and cost substantially.

m: Sending requests with the same prefix to the same replica so the cache hits.

m: Storing the KV cache in fixed pages instead of one contiguous block.
w: vLLM's core trick. It removes the memory fragmentation that wasted most of the cache.

m: Letting finished sequences leave the batch and new ones join mid-flight.
w: Why throughput jumps versus static batching — no waiting for the slowest sequence.

w: How one long request stops blocking everyone else's tokens.

m: A small model drafts several tokens; the big one verifies them in a single pass.
w: Latency reduction with identical output. The follow-up: acceptance rate decides the gain.

m: Flops performed per byte moved from memory.
w: Why decoding is memory-bound and prefill is compute-bound — the key to any serving question.

m: How much your busiest minute exceeds your average.
w: Capacity planning. Provision for the average and you fail every launch.

m: Rejecting requests at the door when the system is saturated.
w: Better than accepting everything and timing out — fail fast and keep the queue honest.

m: Stopping calls to a failing dependency instead of retrying into it.
w: How a slow downstream service takes down everything upstream, and the standard prevention.

w: The number that makes an architecture argument concrete instead of aesthetic.

w: Chunking and context-packing decisions; the constraint that forces retrieval over stuffing.

w: How you answer 'the model got worse last Tuesday' — without it, you cannot.

m: A method for extending a model's context window beyond its trained length.
w: Long-context questions, alongside position interpolation.

w: The simpler long-context extension, usually needing a short fine-tune.

m: The softmaxed query-key products that decide where each token looks.
w: Reading an attention implementation, and any question about what the mask does.

m: Post-training quantisation that compensates for error layer by layer, using sample data.
w: 4-bit weights with small quality loss and no retraining.

m: Quantisation that protects the small fraction of weights that matter most.

m: A 4-bit number format spaced for normally distributed weights.
w: QLoRA's format — it fits the actual distribution of weights rather than spacing values evenly.

m: An 8-bit floating format with real exponent bits, unlike int8.
w: Modern inference on recent hardware. It handles outlier activations that int8 cannot.
